segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Happy new year to everybody. I'm christine grady from the department of bioethics here at the NIH clinical center, and we're going to spend the next hour talking about ethical principles in clinical research.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: These are mostly my views and don't necessarily represent those of the government and I have no conflicts of interest.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: How many of you have studied ethics, you in the room?

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: This may be very familiar territory, hopefully you can have some good questions or additions to the commentary.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So I wanted to start with just a couple of examples of fairly randomly selected from the new england journal of medicine.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: This is a study, double blind placebo controlled randomized study of people with traumatic brain injury seen in the emergency room, given progesterone to see if it made a difference in their symptoms and recovery.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: This was a study that was done without informed consent.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: It was done in an emergency room.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Here's another example of a study looking at children with vasiculo-- can't say the word-- reflux, and again, there was a double blind randomized control study to see if antimicrobials made a difference in some of the reflux.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Another study where the participants were pregnant women, they were randomized to two different time points in terms of thyroid screening and if they screened positive on the tests that were done, they were given thyroxin.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: The outcome, the primary outcome of the study was cognitive ability or i.q.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Actually in their children at the age of 3.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So all recently done study, all published in the new england journal of medicine.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So I think the interesting question to ask ourselves is, are these studies ethical?

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And if you think so, or if you think-- if you're not sure, the question is, how do you make that decision?

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So for the people in the room, what do you think makes studies of the nature that I just showed you ethical or not ethical?

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Any idea? Informed consent? Okay. So we had patients WHO couldn't give informed consent, children WHO legally can't give informed consent, so does that mean two of the three were not ethical?

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Not necessarily, right? Okay. Risk versus benefit, and we didn't go into the details of those, but we'll talk about that in a little bit.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Anything else? Yeah. No actual harm.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Okay. So that's kind of-- falls into the rubric of risk versus benefit.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: I think it's really interesting to think about what does make research ethical.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So that's what we're going to talk about.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: I want to point out a couple things before we go there, though.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: What I often think of as the moral tension or ethical tension in research is pretty much captured by this slide.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: That is that the goal of research, the goal of clinical research, is to generate knowledge, useful knowledge about human health or illness, ways to prevent, diagnose or treat diseases, and the goal is not to benefit the individuals WHO participate in the trial, although

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: at times they do benefit. That sets up the problem ethically, and that is people WHO are asked to participate are actually are the means to developing useful information.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And, therefore, they are at risk of exploitation.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And that's really what a lot of the ethics of clinical research is sort of aimed at attending to.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: We know that sometimes people think of clinical research like this, you know, people WHO participate in research are human guinea pigs.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: They are susceptible to exploitation and sometimes are exploited, but I think it's interesting to think about how we reconcile this.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So what I like to say is that the ethics of clinical research really requires recognizing that there are two parts to this puzzle, that generating useful knowledge is an ethical responsibility, and that knowledge can promote bone fits to society and future patients.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And that that effort of generating useful knowledge for future patients in society has to be constrained by or balanced by, if you prefer the analogy, protecting and respecting the rights and welfare of the people WHO are participating, the participants.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So there's this constant tension between these two, and that's how we think about the ethics of clinical research.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Interestingly over time, over the history of clinical research, there's been interesting changes in how we think about this tension.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So for many years, for hundreds of years, there were very few rules.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Physicians, mostly physicians, experimented for two reasons, one, because they were curious and they had the luxury or the resources to be able to do so, and two, because they wanted to benefit individuals.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: They found individuals that they didn't know what to do about in terms of their illnesses, and so they would experiment on them to try to figure out whether this works or does not work.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: But there were no rules. We went through a-- what people have referred to as a utilitarian era in the united states, maybe in other parts of the world as well, where the emphasis was on benefit to society.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And many of the participants in research during that era were people WHO are now recognized as vulnerable.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: They were-- populations, people in prisons, people in institutions, mentally ill, orphanages, people WHO were seen as not only captive but in some respects, sort of marginal or marginal to society.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And they made them useful by including them in research.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: That led, in the late 60s, early 70s, to a period of time where there was some pretty deep-- of the scope and limitations of research.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So studies that you might be familiar with that sort of led to this level of scrutiny, where all of a sudden people realized for 40 years, we've been studying the natural history of a disease that had a treatment available to it and the

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: people in the study were not getting that treatment.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: It led to a series of congressional hearings, led to an act of research, led to a commission, of behavioral and biomedical research, and then some rules.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And the rules and regulations that we currently operate under were created at that time.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: They started at that time. And prior to that, there were very few rules about how we did research, or very few laws or regulations that had much authority.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: The rules and regulations that were put into place starting around the 70s really had the focus or the emphasis of protecting human subjects, providing lots of procedural rules and other rules that would lead to the protection of human subjects from undue risk from

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: exploitation and would respect their rights through the process of informed consent.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: In the last probably 20 years or so, there has been increased recognition of the possibility of benefit through participation in research.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: This is benefit not just for the individual-- sometimes the individual that participates, but benefit for populations.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So a recognition, for example, that doing research with children sometimes is really important so that we don't end up with therapeutic orphans, people that-- children WHO we don't know how to treat appropriately for certain diseases.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Whereas if we don't include them in research work in clinical practice, making guesses about how to treat children.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So having children participate in research is a benefit to children at large.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: International research has been seen in some cases as beneficial.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And there's lots of ways that research has been seen as not just something to be protected against but beneficial in some ways.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: During this same period of history, and I just went through a lot of history in a very short amount of time, I can answer questions if you want more details, but during the same stretch of history, there are lots of important codes and

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: guidelines that were written and are still-- still have some power.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: I suspect that many of these are familiar to you.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: The nuremberg code was written as part of the nurenburg trials, war crimes, and it still has some influence in terms of how we do research in the world, not just in the united states.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: It's a very distinct code of 10 principles.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: The declaration of helsinki, which came along about 15 years later, was written by the world medical association, which is a group of-- like the american medical association and its equivalent in different countries around the world, and they wrote a document called the declaration

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: of helsinki, which was, some people say, in a little bit of a way a response to nuremberg in the following sense, that it recognized that a lot of research is done by physicians with patients, whereas the nuremberg code was written as a result

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: of research that was done with prisoners in the context of war.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: The declaration of helsinki, as people describe it, is a living document, it's been revised multiple times.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: This slide needs to be updated.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: It was most recently revised in 2013.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And it has a lot of very important pieces to it and a lot of authority around the world.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And I can talk about what those are if you want to know.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: The belmont report is a document that was written by the national commission that I mentioned a few minutes ago, and it's a pretty short, pretty clear exploitation of the principles that underlie the conduct of clinical research.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: I'm going to come back to that in a moment, if you haven't read that, I would say it take the time to do so.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: It's not very long. Then from the WHO, cioms is the council of international organizations of medical sciences, and they, in collaboration with the world health organization, developed international guidelines which were designed to take the principles enunciated in the declaration of helsinki and apply

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: them to the context of doing research in the developing world.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And there are two published versions of those guidelines, 1993 and 2002, and just in the last few months, a revised version is online for people to comment on.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So if you're interested in international research in particular, it's worth taking a look at.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: One of the things I particularly like about the cioms document is in addition to the principles, which many of these have, it has long-- not long, but clear detailed exploitations of how they came up with that principle and what they mean by it.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So it's very useful. In the united states-- is a very influential document in the world.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: It's a good clinical practice, which originally came about through the regulatory agency of the united states, the european union and japan, WHO wanted to find a way to agree on or harmonize the rule under which clinical research could be done so that if

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: you did research in one of those jurisdictions and wanted to have it approved in the other jurisdiction, you have to start all over again.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Which a lot of countries do require.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So ich-gcp has been adopted in a lot of countries around the world.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: -- to speak to specifically to ethics, and it does adopt most of the principles from the declaration of helsinki.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So you can see lots of interaction with this document.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So the belmont report, I mentioned, is a document that was written by the national commission and it has three underlying principles for clinical research: respect for persons, beneficence and justice.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: They take each of these and not only describe what they mean by it, but they also apply it to a specific aspect of clinical-- doing clinical research.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So probably for those of you WHO have ever studied ethics, these are principles that are commonly discussed that don't just apply to clinical research, they apply to lots of things, but the idea of informed consent, they applied beneficence to the idea of risk-benefit

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: assessment and how you make those calculations, and justice to the idea of selecting-- fairly selecting subjects so that there are fair outcomes as well.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: The other important thing the belmont did was describe the difference between clinical research and clinical practice, to sort of make these kinds of distinctions.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So one thing I already alerted you to was the goals.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So the goal of clinical research is to generate useful knowledge.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: The goal of clinical care is not.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: It's to benefit the person or persons in front of you, the persons that are being cared for in the practice.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And you can see how sometimes, those two goals can come into tension and need to be reconciled.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Methods are also very different. So common methods in clinical research.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Talk about double blind trials, placebo controlled trials, health escalation trials of.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: The kinds of things we do all the time in research are very foreign in concept in clinical practice.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: It would be very weird for you to go to your doctor with a sore threat and have the doctor say to you, um, I'm going to give you one of two drugs but neither you nor I are going to know what the drug

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: is, to heal your sore throat.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And yet in research, we do that all the time.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: The other thing is, the other important difference from an ethical perspective is the justification for risk.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: It's clearly not the case in clinical practice, there are risks involved but all of those risks are justified for the potential for the benefit that that intervention offers to that individual WHO is undergoing it.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Whereas in reaccept, we often ask people to do certain things, procedures and interventions, that have no corresponding benefit to them.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: They're really done to answer a question.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So we might ask for an extra biopsy, an extra blood draw, an extra scan.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Pharmacokinetics test. Something like that that exposes people to certain risks, so there's three ways that research and-- clinical research and clinical practice are distinguished and they're very important to keep in mind because they help US answer a lot of questions about what's acceptable

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: and what's not. And the belmont report begins to describe those differences.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: In addition to codes and regulations-- sorry-- codes and guidelines, there are regulations.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So in the united states, there's two important sets of regulations that are worth knowing about.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: One is the common rule. How many of you know about the common rule?

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Okay. The common rule is the-- well, let me start with you have 45 CFR 46, also walking around the halls of this building, sometimes you hear people just talk about it like that, they don't call it the common rule, they call 45 CFR

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: 46. And so 45 CFR 46 is title 45 of the code of federal regulations part46.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And it is the department of health and human services' version of the common rule.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: The regulations for protection of human subjects that anyone getting department of health and human services money has to follow.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: The reason it's called the common rule is that there are 16 other federal agencies that also follow the same set of regulations.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Their regulations are found in different parts of the CFR, not all in title 45, but the content of the rule and the regulation is similar across 16 federal agencies in the united states.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: One of the agencies that does not follow the common rule is FDA.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And FDA has its own set of regulations.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: The regulations that are found at title 21of the CFR are part50 and 56, very similar to what's in the common rule, have a lot of the same requirements, but some important differences.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And then there are other parts of the FDA regulations that are very important for somebody who's doing a treatment ind, for example, or a device trial.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And then there are policies and guidelines that the NIH requires.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So for example, how many of you are investigators?

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: A couple. So if-- how many of you are IRB members?

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Anybody? No. Okay. There are some requirements for inclusion of women and ethnic minorities and children in research that are NIH requirements, but that are-- requirements, I guess, and there are some others that the NIH has that are NIH policy that apply to clinical

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: research. So what does 45 CFR 46 include?

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: There are really three things that are-- there's a lot more than this.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: There's the federal regulations are-- I don't know how many pages, 15 pages, something, of details.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So if you're on an IRB or getting ready to write a study, you might really want to know about what the details are.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: But basically they cover three broad areas.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: One is a lot of description about the composition and function of local institutional review boards, or IRBS.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Another is the criteria that IRBS should use when they're deciding whether or not a study is approvable.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And the third is requirements regarding informed consent of individuals that are going to be included in a study.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So these are spelled out in the common rule and also in 45 CFR 46.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: 45 CFR 46 also has subparts.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Subparts that pertain to additional protections for groups of people that are considered vulnerable for a variety of reasons.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Subpart b refers to fetuses, pregnant women and human in vitro fertilization, c to prisoners and d to children.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And there are some very specific additional requirements that-- entails.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: The FDA regs already mentioned, 21CFR 50 and 56 are very similar to what's found in the common rule, the part50 is about informed consent, part56 is about IRB composition and function.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: There is also a subpart d in the FDA regs that deals with extra protections for research with children.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Then there are ind and ide regulations found in 312 and 812 that are very important for an investigator testing a new investigational drug or device.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So that's a whirlwind through a little with bit of history and a little bit of rules and regulations that exist.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: What I want to spend the rest of the time talking with you about are some sort of conceptual ideas about how you think about research in a way that can help to answer the question of is this research ethical.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And I want to preface it by saying that in our department, some 15 or so years ago now, we realized that a lot of the guidance that's found in the codes and the regulations were developed in response to specific problems.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: They were developed historically at a time that they were responding to some events that happened in history.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And so they have understandably kind of focus on the sort of details of that event that initiated their implementation.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: In addition to, or for the same reason, perhaps, some issues are probably incompletely addressed in some of these guidances, and some of the guidances and regulations are at least interpreted to have divergent recommendations.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So we thought that there was a need for investigators, people WHO are interested in understanding the ethics of research, for people WHO review research, IRB members and others, to have a systematic, coherent and universally applicable framework that they could use to make decisions

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: about-- or make judgments about whether or not a particular research that they were writing or reviewing was ethical.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And so we proposed a seven-principle framework.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: The seven principles-- it's published in a couple of different places.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: The first paper was in 2010, it's also in the textbooks, there's some additions to this and a number of references I could provide to you if you want in some detail, but I'm going to go through it today.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So there's seven principles. They include valuable scientific question, valid scientific methodology, fair subject selection, favorable risk-benefit evaluation, independent review, informed consent, and respect for enrolled subjects.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: One thing before I go into each one of them I want to say is, we didn't make any of these up.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So if you look at the various guidelines and codes, you will find-- of each of these, maybe not exact words, but the concepts and the ideas are there.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: We've just put them together in a way that seems more systematic to US.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: What I mean by that is that it seems right that you have to start at the top.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: You have to answer the question, is this a valuable scientific question, before you go down the list.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So the question of informed consent, informed consent is on there, it's a very important part of doing research, but you don't even get near it until you've gone through lots of other considerations in terms of-- so what does it mean to have a

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: valuable scientific question? So basically what this means is that it has to be worth doing, shorthand for it.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: An ethical clinical research should answer a valuable question, one that will generate new knowledge or understanding about human health or illness, a socially, clinically, or scientifically useful question.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: A good example of this is an article that was written by a very prolific writer in research ethics, benjamin friedman, WHO wrote an article about-- in this article, he was writing about social value in a certain way.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And what he said was he had a nightmare, he was walking down the hall, one of his colleagues said I just successfully transplanted an appendix.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And in the article, benji says-- he kind of scratched his head and he said, well, was that ethical?

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And his colleague responded, well, I got the guy's informed consent.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And he uses that as an example of how informed consent doesn't solve the problem.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: If there wasn't a good reason, a good question to answer by transplanting an appendix, something that you might learn, something you might use to do some important work with, and it wasn't ethical to do it.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And it's an interesting concept because it seems like it is the most important first question to ask: is this research worth doing?

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Now importantly, it doesn't mean that the answer to the question has to be positive.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: You can have negative-- you know, ask a question, get a negative answer, and that's still socially valuable.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: It still gives you information that can be very useful, and in many cases is.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: But if you can't say why this question is worth asking, then you probably have to re-ask yourself, is this research ethical.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: There are many reasons that social value is important.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: The most benefit to society, sort of one side the of the balance that I showed of you before, and it also minimizes exploitation.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: You're asking people to do things for a good reason, not just wasting their time for nothing.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Therefore, it justifies asking them to accept some risk and burden and it's also a responsible way to use resources.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: The second principle in the framework is valid scientific methodology.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And this basically says ethical research should be designed in an ethically rigorous manner.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Of the design, the manner, that will yield valid reliable, generalizable and interpretable data.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So the shorthand here is, you have a question that's worth asking, the second ethical requirement is to design it in a way that you get an answer that you can interpret.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: That you know what you found.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: That you have data that's reasonably understandable.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Again, doesn't have to be positive, it just has to be understandable.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And it has to be designed in a way that's feasible as well.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Now, this requires lots of details, lots of details in choices of end point, choices of design, choices of procedure, statistical method, et cetera.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: You look at this list, some of you might say well, they're all scientific considerations.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: In fact, they are scientific considerations, but every scientific choice that you make has ethical implications.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So designing the study, picking the right outcome, picking the right design to give you the best, most rigorous answers to your question, choosing the precures that will be used to measure outcomes or data points, whatever, and not only planning your statistical methods but

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: managing the data are all ethical requirements of good clinical research.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: There's lots of controversy about this.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Not so much about the idea that things need to be designed in a way that give you a rigorous answer b you how do you balance the best design, the most rigorous design with some of the other things that you need to care

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: about, like the fact that you don't want to-- expose them to excessive risk.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So some of you may have followed the debates that occurred over clinical trials related to ebola in the last year.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: There were a lot of discussions about what's the right kind of design that both gives US an answer to the questions that are so urgently needed to be answered, and respects the rights and the welfare of the participants that are in the trial.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: There's also a lot of really important ethical-- that goes into feasibility.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So if you-- example, are designing a trial where you know you're not going to be able to get the participants that you need to answer it.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: That's sort of ethically a non-starter, because you can't ask some people to accept risk and burden to answer a question that you know you're not going to be able to answer if it's not feasible to get all the people that you need or

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: to get the equipment that you need.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: The third is fair subject selection.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So if a question is worth answering, design, methodology is rigorous and is going to give you an answer that you can make sense out of, now you have to ask the question WHO do I include, WHO do I go after as part of

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: this study? I think critically, especially looking historically, the first guide should be scientific objectives.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Conclusion criteria-- and selection of subjects, and not the fact that people are easily available or vulnerable or marginal or that they are-- either.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: There needs to be a fairness in terms of scientific objectives.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Scientific objective is where you start and then you-- when you're thinking about fair subject selection, there's also a consideration of fairly distributing the harms and benefits.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So let me give you an example.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Let's imagine you think you're doing a study to test a treatment for breast cancer.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Scientifically, you're going to need people in that study WHO have breast cancer, and maybe a very specific type of breast cancer.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: When you're thinking about fairly distributing the harms and the benefits, you may want to -- you may think about, well, which subgroup within the population of people have breast cancer are more susceptible to the kinds of risks that this intervention might have?

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Maybe kidney disease or liver disease or some kinds of things that might need to be used as inclusion criteria in order to reduce the risk and protect some of the subgroups.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: One of my colleagues talks about the best way to think about fair subject selection is to flip it on its head.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: In other words, not start with WHO scientifically should you include in the study, but start with the idea that everybody should be included unless there's a reason to exclude them, justification for excluding them.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So then the question becomes what are-- justification for excluding people?

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: One might be that they can't help answer the question, they don't meet the scientific objective.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Another might be that they are at higher risk than everybody else, and a third and very important one is they may be more vulnerable than other populations and, therefore, we should think about whether we need to include them at the front end.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: I understand there will be another lecture, a whole lecture on vulnerability, so I won't say more about that, but if you have questions, we can talk about that.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: I think it's important to go back to something i've already alluded to, and that is in thinking about distributing or fair distribution of the risks and benefits, it's important to keep in mind this sort of pendulum swing that's been occurring between thinking of

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: research as always a burden, always subject to-- always in need of protection.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And the sort of opposite swing of the pendulum, where research can be or is in many cases a benefit, and subjects need and want access.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So thinking about your risks and benefits, you need to keep in mind those different-- and where any particular project might fall.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: If you've got a question worth asking, a design that's rigorous, selecting the appropriate-- given scientist objectives, vulnerability, and now the question is, what's the risk-benefit look like?

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: For the participants in the study.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So this is a sort of different kind of risk-benefit analysis than the first one, which is, is the study worth doing?

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: In a study that's worth doing, there are still ways that one can make sure that the risk to the individuals in the study are minimized and necessary.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So you may see a proposal, for example, that asks to do, you know, 10 mris over the source of six months.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So an interesting question to ask is, are 10 necessary, or could the question be answered by doing 6or 5or, you know, spreading them out over a further amount of time?

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Are there other ways to minimize the burden of those procedures to the participants?

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Are there risks to the individuals in the study justified by either benefit to them or potential benefit to them, or-- and/or the importance of the knowledge, the social value.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And are benefits enhanced, are there ways to enhance benefits in the process of doing research.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And these are pretty normal understandable questions, no big deal, but the process of doing it is not so straightforward.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Justification about risk, for example, there's an interesting challenge in terms of defining what is a risk in research, how do we know how bad this risk is or how to think about this risk?

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And there are certainly lots of reasons to think about both probability and magnitude of risk, and different types of risk.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So one of the things the regulations talk about is physical, psychological, social, financial risk.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: It's interesting to think about how often in research you consider financial risk.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Some people talk about-- i've had questioned raised that fall into the certain sort of categories.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: If somebody has to travel through a very tough neighborhood or park really far away from the clinic and walk to the clinic and there's some hazards in that walk, are those risks of research, or are those separate from the risks of research?

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: How do we take those things into account when making an assessment of what the risks are.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And I think importantly, in all cases of research, there is some uncertainty about risk.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And if there wasn't some uncertainty about risk, we probably wouldn't be doing the research because part of doing research is helping to identify either what the risks are, the magnitude of the risks, the comparative risks, or some other nuance about the risk.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So defining risks and measuring risks is a very important part of figuring this out but it's not easy in many cases.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Minimizing risk is also something that we need to pay attention to and sometimes things are very straightforward, as I mentioned already, reducing the number of procedures, other things that people talk about are doing procedures that are clinically required, and in other words, instead

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: of asking for additional blood for research purposes, have it drawn at the time when clinical bloods are being drawn.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Making sure that the people WHO are doing procedures have the right kind of training.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So there are lots of really important, sometimes very obvious, ways to minimize risk.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And limiting risk really gets down to how we protect certain groups of people.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So one of the ways, for example, that the regulations regarding the research with children work is it limits the amount of risk that children can be exposed to in research.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Minimal risk procedures in research for children is basically-- we're generally fine.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: More risk can be expected when there's benefit for the children in the study, and then the rule for anything more than a minimal risk without -- are much more stringent and in some cases research cannot be done.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: There's also similar challenges in terms of defining benefits.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: If you have a certain kind of serious illness, and there are few interventions available to treat that illness, and you are entering a study in which there's an intervention being offered, is that, by definition, a prospective benefit?

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Is it only an-- phase 3versus phase 1, for example, how do we decide what the prospect of benefit is in some cases?

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And a lot of information distinguishing what are called direct benefits versus secondary.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So the direct benefit to our-- in a-- possible therapeutic benefit that one might derive from an intervention.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: The secondary benefits might be other medical care that you might receive because of the study, payment that you might receive as part of a study, feeling like you're contributing to society that might be psychologically beneficial, consider a secondary benefit.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So importantly, going back to my original balancing scale, most guidance recognizes that interests other than the subject,, research in which we know in advance the individual participating will not benefit, there's no prospect of benefit, can sometimes be ethically acceptable, as long as the

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: rights of the individuals WHO are participants have been adequately protected.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So the question worth asking, a design that's rigorous, the right population chosen, efforts made to minimize risks and enhance benefits, now the next thing on that list is independent review.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And so this is a process which allows an investigator or a research team WHO has investments in research to have somebody else say, is this acceptable.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: To ensure that the ethical requirements have been fulfilled, check any biases that the investigator might bring, and assure the public.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So most research in the united states is independently-- by an institutional review board, IRB.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: There's-- the methods of reviewing. Most countries around the world have an equivalent kind of ethics research review committee that looks at research before it starts.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Criteria that are found both in the common rule and the FDA regulations that the IRB is supposed to use in order to determine whether a particular study is approvable, include these.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And you'll see flavors of things that i've already talked about.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: That risks were minimized, there's more to that statement than on the slide.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: That risks are justified by any institute that benefits subjects or the importance of the knowledge, that subjects will be selected and treated fairly, and that informed consent was adequate.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: There are lots of interesting challenges in the news right now, many IRBS have huge volume of protocol.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: How many of you have ever been to an IRB meeting?

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Okay. So oftentimes an IRB meeting can last four hours, but you have maybe 10 protocols.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Some of them, protocols sometimes are 300 pages long and dense in terms of their scientific background, et cetera.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So the challenge is not trivial in terms of understanding what it's about, having a process of asking questions often of the investigator, and find these principles and thinking about, well, is this something that's-- in its current form?

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Consequently there's been plenty of evidence to show that IRBS are can-- tend to be inconsistent.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: This has created problems in particular for multicenter studies or multisite studies, so if you have a study that has 100 different sites, oftentimes 100 different ir bs have to review it, and they may have to have either grossly different decisions or sometimes just

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: mildly different decisions but that impact the entire spectrum.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So this is a problem that a lot of people have talked about, and lots of attention right now to using single IRB review for multisite studies.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: This year, in september of 2015, the department of health and human services published what's called a notice of proposed rulemaking, that's what nprm stands for, maybe some of you have heard about it, and basically it's a proposal for changing the common rule.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And there's some very interesting-- some minor and some huge changes in terms of what they're proposing.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: One of them is this, that for multicenter studies, domestic, not international, a single IRB review will be required.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: It won't be required to have different institutions reviewing-- different institutions, ir bs reviewing the study, but there's a lot of consternation about how this is going to look, whether it will be adequately protective and how you'll make arrangements to-- institutions-- so the sixth

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: of the seven on our list is informed consent.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: As someone in the audience said, a lot of people, when they think about sort of abstractly, what is it that makes-- sorry-- research ethical, clinical research ethical, the answer often is informed consent, and certainly in most cases, informed consent is an important part

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: of doing ethical research. But what's interesting about it is, if you think about it, until you have a proposal that's worth doing and well designed and you've minimized risk and have somebody else review it, there is no reason to ask somebody for their

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: informed consent. You don't even get there until-- but informed consent, once you're there, has a goal of making sure that the people that you're offering participation to have an opportunity to decide whether they want to participate or continue to participate, and whether or

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: not the participating is compatible with their goals and their interests and their values.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: A really important concept. Most of the documents, the code guidelines, regulations, have something related to informed consent.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Some of them are very strong.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So nuremberg code is famously quoted as saying-- the voluntary consent of the human subject is absolutely essential.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: The cioms guidelines says for all biomedical research involving human subjects, the investigator must obtain the informed consent of the prospective subject or authorized representative.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: There are some exceptions, there are some ways to waive informed consent, emergencies are one example, so the study I showed you at the beginning where you're encountering and doing-- on people in the emergency room WHO have traumatic brain injury, there's a process that's

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: regulatorily described that one needs to go through in order to do that, but those kinds of research can sometimes be done without getting the consent of the individuals WHO are in a position, for the most part, to not be able to give informed

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: consent. So what does informed consent involve?

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: It involved a number of steps, disclosure of information, understanding the information well enough to make a decision, a choice that they can make, which is hopefully voluntary, in other words, not forced or unduly influenced by others or other factors.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And then they authorize it. I don't know if you can see my picture, the cartoon which is not really that funny.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: People standing around the table looking at a guy who's being asked to sign consent and you can see them with their trench coats and their hats, putting the pressure on this poor guy who's sweating.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Unfortunately, sometimes informed consent includes-- like that or feels like that to people.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Other times, it's done, you know, in a very open and iterative way so that people really can engage with the information, ask question, understand it and make a decision.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: There are lots of challenges to this.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: You can tell i've spent a lot of time thinking about it, i've done some of my research on informed consent, but for example, just think about how many of you have seen consent forms that are used in the intramural program?

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Any of you? So oftentimes, not always, the consent form-- 15, 18 pages long.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Those are long documents. Choice is about what to put in those consent documents and how to state things are really very ethically important and very difficult.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: To be able to give people the information without making it so long and so cumbersome that they -- absorb it.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Then the IRB has an important role in reviewing consent, both the plan for informing-- about various aspects of a study, how investigators of the research team are going to know whether or not somebody understands, and whether their choice is voluntary.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So the seventh of our seven principle framework is what we call respect for-- subjects.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: This is an element or a principle that I think really needs some more work.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Let me tell you where it came from first and then why I say it needs more work.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So in reviewing the documents, the codes of ethics, the literature on research ethics, the regulations, they all talk about what you do up front.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: You get review, you make sure the risks and benefits are justified and risks are minimized, and get a person's informed consent, and then your study begins.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And much of the guidance, not all of it but much of the guidance doesn't say much else about what happens.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: That doesn't make any sense, right?

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Your ethical obligation to people that you're enrolling in research can't end the minute you get their informed consent, right?

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: You still have obligations to people.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And so these obligations include at least things like protecting their confidentiality, monitoring their welfare, recognizing the that they have a white to withdraw, providing them new information as it becomes available that might affect their decision to participate, informing them of your findings, planning

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: for what happens at the end of the trial.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: There are other things that are not on this list.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Compensation for research related injury. There are a lot of things that people do talk about that are sort of in this-- under this rubric of what happens after the study begins.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So I think both-- hopefully you can see why this is an important element but also you can see why there needs to be more work on this because some of these things are done without a lot of guidance.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: There is some guidance, so for example, in the nuremberg-- sometimes should be at liberty to bring the experiment to an end, to withdraw at any time.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Helsinki talks about privacy and confidentiality and minimizing the impact of the study on a person's physical and mental integrity.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So those are the seven. Hopefully they made some sense.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: I think importantly, again, i've said this but, you know, we think of them as systematic and sequential.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So you start at the top and work your way down, and that that's necessary, so when you're thinking about a study, whether you're writing it, reviewing it, entering as a participant, it's worth thinking about them one at a time and saying okay, does

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: this study have value, is it well designed, are the right people being asked to participate, the inclusion criteria-- has it been reviewed by an IRB?

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: If there are good processes in place for informed consent.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And are all the things that happen to people, once the study starts, the monitoring, the confidentiality, the plans for what happens in the end, are those all adequate?

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And you can ask those questions for every single study that you consider in any way.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: It also seems important to recognize that these can be universal.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: In other words, they apply to all studies everywhere across town.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: What's important, however, is thinking about how they're actually manifested.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So risk, for example, might vary over time from one time point or another or to one geographic location to another.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: The method in which you disclose information in informed consent, might vary by population.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Doesn't mean-- the principle of giving people the operation that they can use to make a decision, it's how you implement it that changes the study.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And, of course, they're going to require some balancing and specifying.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So the idea of having an adequate justification for the risk requires a lot of specification in terms of determining what are the risks, what are the risks that count in this case, how do we balance them with the benefits, what are the benefits

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: that count in this case. How do we weigh them, how do we balance them against the rigor of the study?

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And there are a lot of interesting examples of challenges, for example n randomized controlled trials, people worry about things like randomizing people.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Especially if one of the arms to which people might be randomized is a placebo arm.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: We worry about that from a placebo perspective, and yet if the question is worth asking and the design is rigorous, it might be that placebo is the best way to answer the question, and not only the best way to answer the question but

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: the fairest thing for the individual, because if you know up front that the drug is better than placebo, then maybe you shouldn't be doing the study.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So it's that kind of balancing that needs to be done.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: In order to apply those principles and reconcile the inherent conflicts and make informed judgments about ethical research, you need people WHO are investigators and research teams and IRB members, et cetera, WHO have this kind of-- use this kind of a framework so hopefully

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: all of you will be able to find it useful-- I want to end with just a minute or two about some interesting challenges that are going on that people have-- some of these actually are referred to in the nprm in the proposals to

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: changing the common rule, but certain ways that we do research now that were not envisioned when some of the regulations and code of ethics were written, so people are beginning to question, do we have the right set of guidance in terms of doing

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: research. I think the principles-- the seven principles that he just described are very useful in thinking through these new challenges of research.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: But for example, more and more of the research that's being done is multisite and also multi-national.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So you have differences between sites, differences between countries that make very important challenges in terms of how to do something right that's also scientifically rigorous.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: We've already mentioned the IRB challenges in terms of multiple sites.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: There's been a lot of attention in the last couple of years to learning healthcare systems,, quality improvement, comparative research, usual care research and whether or not these are similar to the clinical trial paradigms that the regulations and the guidance was written about.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And there are huge debates in the literature, maybe some of you have heard of the study a couple years ago, there are still people writing that-- report study in terms of whether or not we have the right paradigm to thinking about research ethics.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Also in the middle of lots of debate about research using data, samples, biospecimens, the notice of proposed rulemaking, the nprm, has some major changes in terms of how we do research-- somehow we currently do research that require assessments and data.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: There are lots of questions about whether or not the nprm proposals are correct and how they're going to change how we do research.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And certainly much attention in the last couple of years to genomic data, selecting genomic data and sharing genomic data.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: One of the other NIH policies that's very influential is the genomic data sharing policy, that requires NIH funded investigators to-- genomic research to share the data in-- so lots of interesting challenges in the changing-- this last slight is just a link to some

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: more information that you might find useful.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So questions, comments, challenges? Nothing. Clear as mud?

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Those of you WHO studied ethics in the past, did this add anything to your knowledge base or was this repetitious?

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Nobody has any questions, any cases you want to raise?

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Things you've been wondering about? Did you have a question?

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: what do you mean by if I understand what you mean correctly, most of the time, especially for studies that involve intervention, there's a pretty thorough history and physical done, careful assessment of whether each individual meets the inclusion criteria that are specified to protect

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: people in that study, and then a series of data points at which different measurements are taken to see how the individual is or is not responding to the intervention.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Which includes not only, you know, measures of efficacy, if you will, but also safety, what kinds of toxicity, side effects, et cetera.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So those are in research, especially research interventions, those are very carefully monitored, those kinds of things.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Is that what you had in mind?

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: that's a good question. It is the nature of the beast that we don't know the full effect of things that we're trying in research, why we are monitoring so closely and watching people.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And almost every study that you might encounter has what they call stopping rules, which are both for individuals if individuals experience this kind of side effect or this level of side effect, they will be taken out of the study or their dose will

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: be adjusted or withheld for a while, and there are also stopping rules usually for entire study.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Two people have this it-- four people have this kind of level of side effect and the study will be changed or stopped or things like that.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So those kinds of safeguards are built into studies all the time.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: However, there's another issue that I think you're raising, and that is, what if somebody is hurt?

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And it is one of the more controversial areas, and that is that in the united states anyway, we do not have a requirement for or a system for compensating people WHO are hurt in research or injured in research.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: What we do have is a regulation that requires investigators to tell people what will happen if they get hurt in research, and so consent forms often have language that says something like if you are injured as part of this research or if you

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: are hurt as part of this research, we will take care of you for a short-term or we will transfer you to someplace else that will be able to take care of you, but your insurance company will pay for that.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So we don't have a good system.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: And that's something that's been a-- I think a-- it has been contentious because most people WHO think about it for more than a few minutes think that's a mistake, we ought to have a system in place for helping people WHO are hurt.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: There's lots of literature on that.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Other questions? Well, then, go forth.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Remember, we have the department of bioethics which offers consults and classes and we have ethics grand rounds four times a year, discussions, so please take advantage of US.
